vignette:
He arrives for sessions still dressed in the same dark polo shirt and khakis he wears every day, a uniform that requires no decisions. The office air conditioning hums, and he sits at the edge of the chair, hands clasped, eyes fixed on a spot on the wall just above my left shoulder. When I ask how his week went, he says, "Fine," and then waits. The silence is not hostile, but careful-like a software engineer checking every variable before a compile.

The story he tells comes out in fragments, sometimes in the same session, sometimes across weeks. Four years ago, he was a senior developer at a mid-sized tech firm, respected for his clean code and quiet reliability. A colleague-younger, also male, someone he trusted as a friend over late-night debugging sessions-invited him to a private apartment after a team dinner to "talk about a new project." He went. Inside, the conversation turned. The colleague mocked his bachelor lifestyle, his immigrant accent, then moved closer. He froze. When the assault happened, he did not fight, did not scream. He just kept repeating, "No," in a voice that barely left his throat. Afterwards, he walked home, showered, and went to work the next morning without telling anyone.

Now, in the present, that colleague has transferred to another city, but he still sees a face in the elevator that could be his. His heart hammers, his vision narrows, and the next several seconds vanish. He takes the stairs for months, even though his knees ache. He switched teams to avoid collaborative projects. He now works exclusively from home, logging in at 6 a.m. and logging off at 10 p.m. because the boundaries feel safer than the emptiness of afternoons. His code has grown slower, more defensive-he writes extra null checks, wraps everything in try-catch blocks, as if preparing for errors that might never come. His manager once commented that he seemed distracted. He didn't respond.

Sleep is a battleground. He lies in bed rigid, listening to his own breathing, replaying the sound of that colleague's voice, the weight of hands, the metallic taste of his own silence. Nightmares visit most nights-not always about the assault, but about being trapped in small rooms, about losing control of a car, about drowning. He wakes with his fists clenched and a headache that lasts all day. Caffeine only makes it worse, but he cannot stop.

He has stopped dating. The last time he tried, a kind woman from a community center touched his arm while laughing, and he recoiled so violently that she spilled her tea. He apologized, but never called her again. He no longer attends Friday prayers at the mosque because the closeness of bodies in the prayer row triggers a tightness in his chest. When his mother calls from overseas, he tells her everything is fine, just busy with work. He avoids mirrors, especially in the morning, because the face that looks back feels foreign-someone who let it happen.

His PCL-5 score was 77, meaning every question was a high endorsement. He acknowledges that he thinks about the assault constantly, even when he is staring at his monitor or washing dishes. He avoids any intimacy, any vulnerability. He feels numb, detached from others, and guilty that he cannot "just get over it," as a cousin once told him. He wants to forget, but his mind has become a system that cannot flush its own cache.

In session, his voice is flat when he recounts these details. But when I say, "That must have been unbearable alone," his fingers uncurl slightly, and for a moment, his gaze meets mine.
